newsitem.title: USA: Clinton hopeful on budget, worried about tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Clinton hopeful on budget, worried about tax cuts.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Friday he was optimistic about the chances for an accord with Congress to balance the budget by 2002, but insisted tax cuts not be allowed to "explode" the deficit afterwards.
Clinton, a Democrat, sent two top aides to Capitol Hill to try to resolve remaining differences over taxes and spending with the Republican-controlled Congress on a budget agreement.

As described by officials, the deal under discussion would cut spending across the government over five years, notably in the Medicare and Medicaid health care programmes, and offer $85 billion in tax cuts to benefit investors and families.
Clinton said he was optimistic on the chances for a deal, which aims to balance the budget for the first time since 1969, but suggested that taxes remain a bone of contention.
"I am very optimistic. I am very hopeful," Clinton said as he made a statement hailing news that the unemployment rate fell to 4.9 percent in April, its lowest level since 1973.
"The one thing I am determined to do is to keep on this economic course which has brought us the lowest unemployment rate in 24 years," he added.

"We have to be very careful not to set conditions in motion which could explode the deficit again because of the way the tax cut is written or other provisions are written after this budget period ends," he said.

White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin went to Capitol Hill on Friday morning to resume negotiations, with Bowles suggesting that progress had been made on the tax cut issues, which he called "minor."
White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters that other issues were unresolved, adding the White House was ready for all contingencies, including announcing a deal, or not.
A House of Representatives Republican source said that the current difficulty in reaching an agreement had to do with a White House request for additional spending.
"If this thing falls apart, it's because the White House wants more spending," the source said, declining to be named.

If the White House and the congressional Republicans come to an agreement among themselves, the other difficult problem they will face will be to sell the pact to their own parties, both of which have factions who oppose the outlined pact.
The proposed deal's $85 billion tax cut over five years was expected to include reductions in capital gains and estate taxes and a $500 child tax credit, officials said.
Much of the government's five-year savings would come from the Medicare health care programme for the elderly. Its spending would fall by $115 billion through 2002.

Savings of over $20 billion would come from the Medicaid health care programme for the poor. Other domestic programmes would be cut $68 billion and defence by about $80 billion from the amount that would be spent under current policies.
However, Clinton would receive $32 billion in spending for his education, environment and other new initiatives.
The Democratic White House and Republican Congress have been at loggerheads over the budget since Republicans won majority control of both U.S. legislative chambers in 1994.
The two sides failed to reach a balanced budget agreement over the ensuing two years, leading to two partial shut-downs of the federal government in late 1995 and early 1996.

Having won re-election in 1996, Clinton is eager to reach a budget agreement as a cornerstone of his administration's achievements, but he also wants to avoid being criticised for the spending cuts it will inevitably entail.
Republicans, for their part, want both sharper spending cuts than Clinton may like as well as deeper tax cuts.
